prompt.context: Our client is an American payphone company that installs and maintains payphones in commercial and residential buildings. Payphones is a dying business globally. The client has contacted us to help figure out how they can preserve and improve profitability in existing business for as long as possible. The CEO has already communicated that the firm is not interested in entering new markets or adding more services to this business.
prompt.question: How can the client preserve and improve profitability in their existing payphone business?

clarifying_info.q: How do they make money? / Do they share profits with the builder?
clarifying_info.a: Once our client gets a contract from the builder to install a payphone, all the costs and revenues are attributed to the client. The builder is not involved post the initial contract phase.

clarifying_info.q: How do you collect revenues from the phone?
clarifying_info.a: In addition to revenues from initial installations, coins are collected from traditional payphones when the coin box is full.

exhibits.title: Profitability Framework Tree
exhibits.shows: A profit tree breaking down revenues and costs for the payphone business
exhibits.data: Revenue branch: # of phones installed, Revenue per phone (Life of phone in years, Revenue per year broken into # of callers per year x Avg. Call value = # minutes x Avg. Charge/minute). Costs branch: Variable costs (# Phones x Costs per phone = Upfront [Cost of phone, Installation costs: Labor/testing] + Maintenance [Regular Coin collection labor, Phone provider bill, Technical support]), Fixed costs (Salaries, Other General & Admin).

framework: Revenues: number of phones installed x revenue per phone per year x life of phone
Revenue per phone = number of callers per year x average call value (minutes x charge per minute)
Variable costs per phone: upfront costs (device cost + installation labor/testing) + maintenance costs (coin collection labor, phone provider bill, technical support)

Key levers given CEO constraint (no new markets/services): focus on cost reduction — upfront device cost, maintenance efficiency, coin-collection labor, network provider contract negotiation, and SG&A

questions.prompt: Question 1: What ideas do you have to increase profits for the client?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a profitability framework identifying revenue and cost drivers. Recognize this is a mature/dying business so revenue growth levers (more phones, more users, more calls) are limited. Focus should shift to cost reduction: reduce cost of phone devices (refurbished/old phones), decrease maintenance costs, lower phone downtime, negotiate network provider contracts, reduce coin-collection labor frequency, cut SG&A.

questions.prompt: Question 2: The client has two options to reduce upfront device cost. Option 1 — Microchip phone: brand new, microchip tells maintenance when coin box is full, no downtime. Option 2 — Refurbished phone: traditional technology, forecasting department schedules coin collection visits (coin box historically half full on each visit), 10 days downtime per year. Which phone would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for cost and revenue data for both phones. Key factors: device cost, revenue per day, coin box capacity, downtime days, labor cost per visit, network provider cost per year, phone life. Calculate annual revenue, number of coin-collection visits, annual maintenance cost, annual contribution, total profit over phone life, and breakeven period for microchip phone vs refurbished phone.

math.setup: Assume 360 days/year. Microchip phone: device $700, revenue/day $2, coin box capacity $72, 0 downtime days, labor $10/visit, network $100/year, life 10 years. Refurbished phone: device $200, revenue/day $2, coin box capacity $72, 10 downtime days/year, labor $10/visit, network $100/year, life 10 years.
steps: Coin-collection visits/year: Microchip = $720 / $72 = 10 (box always full); Refurb = 2 x ($700 / $72) = ~20 (box only half full each visit, so twice as many visits needed)
Maintenance cost/year: Microchip = 10 x $10 = $100; Refurb = 20 x $10 = $200
Profit over life (10 years): Microchip = $520 x 10 - $700 = $4,500; Refurb = $400 x 10 - $200 = $3,800
Breakeven for microchip vs refurb: ($700 - $200) / ($520 - $400) = $500 / $120 = 4.2 years
math.answer: Microchip phone total profit = $4,500; Refurbished phone total profit = $3,800. Microchip phone is more profitable over the phone life. Breakeven vs refurbished = 4.2 years.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Do you think the new high-tech microchip option or the old refurbished phone option is better? Why?
questions.guidance: No single correct answer; tests business acumen. One strong response: it may not make sense to install new phones given the 4.2-year breakeven relative to a dying technology — payphones may not remain viable for 10 years. An alternative: improving the forecasting for the old phones to reduce visits (moving from half-full to full-box collections) would close most of the profitability gap without the higher upfront investment.

questions.prompt: Question 4: In order to generate new revenue, the client has asked us to look for places where more payphones can be installed across the US. How would you come up with the list?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure ideas in a MECE way. Key insight: people use payphones when they (a) do not own a cell phone, (b) cannot use a cell phone (no network, dead battery, no minutes), or (c) are not allowed to use cell phones. Use this to drive location categories.

brainstorming.prompt: What are MECE categories of locations where more payphones could be installed in the US?

categories.name: Commercial buildings — restricted cell use
ideas: Private companies with strict data-security policies

categories.name: Residential buildings
ideas: Phone booths in remote or rural locations with poor cell coverage

recommendation: Prioritize cost reduction over revenue growth given the dying-market context and CEO constraint on new markets

In the near term, focus on improving coin-collection forecasting for refurbished phones to reduce maintenance visits and close the profitability gap with microchip phones — without incurring the higher upfront cost
If the business is expected to last well beyond 4.2 years, consider microchip phones selectively for high-revenue locations where the breakeven can be recovered
risks: Improving forecasting without a buffer could occasionally result in a full coin box and phone downtime, reducing revenue
Payphone viability may shorten below the 10-year phone life, eroding the microchip phone investment
next_steps: Conduct in-depth competitor and market analysis to identify remaining new installation opportunities
Pilot improved coin-collection forecasting on a subset of refurbished phones and measure actual visit reduction
Evaluate network provider contract renegotiation to reduce the $100/year per-phone cost
